result: VHH123 and VHH188 are specific for mouse and human TfR, respectively, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface proteins as demonstrated by immunoblot, LC/MS/MS, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins, and flow cytometry. Contaminants co-immunoprecipitated were predominantly cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins not accessible in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 provide convergent evidence from multiple orthogonal methods (immunoblot, LC/MS/MS, SDS-PAGE, flow cytometry) demonstrating specificity. C67-C68 address potential contamination concerns and appropriately dismiss them based on subcellular localization. The multi-method validation approach is rigorous and the conclusion is well-supported.

result: Anti-TfR nanobodies enable non-invasive tracking of transplanted cells by PET/CT without genetic modification. VHH123 tracks mouse cells in Tfrchu/hu recipients, while VHH188 tracks Tfrchu/hu cells in C57BL/6 recipients. The congenic mouse pair with species-specific VHHs provides a unique tool for transplant studies of any TfR-expressing proliferating cells.
evaluation: Claims C106-C112 provide direct experimental evidence of bone marrow transplant tracking with appropriate controls (C109). The timing considerations (C111) and feasibility conclusions (C112) are well-supported by the data. Claims C122-C124 and C154-C155 appropriately summarize the utility of the system. This represents a core finding of the manuscript.

result: 89Zr and 64Cu chelated to anti-TfR nanobodies are released upon endocytosis due to exposure to low endosomal pH. At later timepoints (≥24 hr), PET signals predominantly reflect free radioisotope accumulation in mineralized bone (89Zr) rather than TfR distribution. This release is unique to anti-TfR VHHs and not observed with VHHs targeting other surface markers.
evaluation: Claims C72-C79 provide strong evidence from matched vs. unmatched VHH/mouse pairs, ex vivo measurements of flushed bone marrow vs. bone matrix, and ROI analysis. C84-C85 provide critical negative controls with non-TfR VHHs. C86-C88 establish the pH-dependent mechanism in vitro. The conclusion (C101, C104) that isotope release is an unavoidable consequence of TfR binding is well-supported by converging evidence.

result: Comparison of 89Zr, 64Cu, and 18F-labeled anti-TfR VHHs reveals distinct kinetics and signal patterns. At 1 hr post-injection, all three isotopes show specific bone marrow accumulation. 18F provides sharper images but has limited observation window (<12 hr) due to short half-life. 64Cu shows liver accumulation at later timepoints due to slow release from NOTA. Isotope choice must consider target tissues and experimental time scale.
evaluation: Claims C89-C98 provide systematic comparison of three radioisotopes with appropriate time-course imaging. C92-C95 correctly identify the trade-off between image quality and observation window for 18F. C96-C97 document 64Cu-specific liver accumulation with mechanistic explanation. C102-C103 provide quantitative ROI analysis supporting the conclusions. C105 appropriately summarizes practical implications.

result: VHH123 can image B16.F10 melanoma cells transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients. At 4 weeks post-transplantation, clear lung signals were observed with VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu, significantly higher than non-specific anti-GFP control. Necropsy confirmed melanotic tumors in lungs. ROI analysis on lung and heart is less precise due to breathing and cardiac motion.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 provide direct evidence of tumor detection with appropriate negative control (C116) and necropsy confirmation (C117). C113-C114 establish expected timeline. C118 shows significant difference by ROI analysis. C120-C121 appropriately acknowledge limitations of lung imaging due to motion artifacts. The tumor tracking application is well-demonstrated.

result: VHH188 produces intense signal in placentas of C57BL/6 mice carrying Tfrchu/wt embryos, but not in embryonic tissues. TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter fetal tissue. Notably, no free 89Zr release was observed in placenta, departing from all other imaging experiments. This may reflect unique pH conditions or absence of release co-factors in syncytiotrophoblast-I.
evaluation: Claims C127-C129 provide strong evidence with appropriate controls (C128) and statistical significance (C129). C132 confirms signal originates from placenta, not embryo, through ex vivo imaging. C133-C134 document the surprising absence of 89Zr release. C178-C180 offer plausible mechanistic hypotheses but acknowledge uncertainty. The placental barrier finding is novel and well-documented, though the mechanism remains speculative.

result: Anti-TfR radiotracers show no observable CNS accumulation by PET/CT but demonstrate CNS accumulation by ex vivo radiospectrometry. The lack of PET signal is attributed to low CNS concentrations (1-5% of plasma), radioisotope release post-internalization, and potential impediment by PEGylation. Gamma ray spectrometry confirmed accumulation in CNS of appropriate genotype.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C80-C81 clearly document the discrepancy between PET imaging and ex vivo measurements. C82 cites prior work supporting BBB crossing capability. C83 and C164-C167 provide plausible explanations for the negative PET signal. C168 provides confirmatory ex vivo data. The conclusion that VHHs cross the BBB but at levels below PET detection threshold is well-supported.

result: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F through click chemistry avoids radioisotope release complications but comes with trade-offs including short half-life (<12 hr observation window), expensive synthesis, and typical accumulation in elimination organs (gall bladder, GI tract) when using TCO-tetrazine chemistry.
evaluation: Claims C60 and C183 correctly identify the advantage of covalent 18F labeling. C61 and C184 appropriately document the limitations with supporting citations. The trade-off analysis is balanced and well-supported by both the current data and cited literature.

result: Nanobodies offer superior properties for PET imaging compared to intact immunoglobulins, including small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, shorter circulatory half-life (~30 min vs. several days), and improved signal-to-noise ratio. PEGylation further improves contrast by reducing renal clearance. Chemo-enzymatic methods enable site-specific modification with chelators and click handles.
evaluation: These claims summarize well-established advantages of nanobodies for imaging applications, appropriately supported by citations (C30-C32, C147-C148, C150-C151). The properties are stated as general knowledge in the field rather than novel findings of this study. All claims are properly referenced.

result: Current cell tracking methods have various limitations: fluorescence/luminescence methods suffer from limited depth penetration and require invasive surgery for cellular resolution; NMR lacks specificity; SPECT/PET lack single-cell resolution but enable non-invasive whole-body imaging. Methods for detecting tumors of mouse origin in their natural host are limited. Most approaches require genetic modification or cell-specific markers.
evaluation: These claims provide appropriate background context for the study, summarizing limitations of existing methods. All claims are properly supported by citations (C16-C24, C137, C139-C142, C152). C153 correctly identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current work. This represents standard literature review rather than novel findings.

result: TfR (CD71, encoded by Tfrc) is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein near-ubiquitously expressed, particularly on proliferating cells including many tumors. TfR mediates iron uptake through transferrin endocytosis and recycling. TfR is expressed at the BBB and placental barrier for iron delivery. Anti-TfR nanobodies can traverse the BBB, but placental crossing has not been explored.
evaluation: These claims provide essential background on TfR biology, all appropriately supported by citations (C37-C40, C47-C48). C41-C43 describe the well-established TfR trafficking pathway. C44-C46 document TfR expression at barrier sites with proper citations. C49 correctly identifies a knowledge gap addressed by the study. This represents accurate literature review.

result: The Tfrchu/hu mouse model (Jackson Labs strain 038212) expresses a chimeric TfR with human ectodomain (amino acids 196-381, 74% identity to mouse). Combined with species-specific anti-TfR VHHs, this constitutes a congenic pair ideally suited for transplant experiments. The system enables tracking of mouse tumors in Tfrchu/hu mice and human PDX models in wild-type mice without genetic modification. Production of nanobody tracers is relatively simple.
evaluation: Claims C53, C62, and C163 provide specific details about the mouse model with proper citations. C158-C162 appropriately describe the advantages and applications of the system. C187-C188 make reasonable claims about accessibility and utility. The characterization of the model and its applications is well-supported.

result: The mechanism of 89Zr release may involve a TfR-specific co-factor beyond acidic pH. Release of free 89Zr from DFO after epitope-binding should be a concern for clinical development. The 'free 89Zr signal pattern' may be traded for increased liver signal by using 64Cu instead.
evaluation: Claims C174-C176 are explicitly speculative ("may also be consistent," "perhaps," "may shed further light"). C175 proposes an unidentified co-factor without direct evidence. C181 makes a reasonable extrapolation to clinical applications. C182 offers a practical alternative supported by cited literature. The mechanistic speculation is acknowledged as uncertain by the authors.
